Worksheet 3 | SL Build

Build the Canteen Orders Database

Open a blank workspace and build the whole database yourself. This worksheet gives you the schema, the ERD, and a small starter dataset. You then create the tables in the correct order, load rows in batches, and finish with UPDATE and DELETE.

CREATE TABLE Composite key INSERT UPDATE DELETE
Open Blank Workspace All SQL worksheets

Build Goal

  • Create CUSTOMER, PRODUCT, ORDER_HEADER, and ORDER_ITEM
  • Use a composite key in ORDER_ITEM
  • Load only a small starter dataset, then test it

Syllabus Links

  • A3.2.4 table construction with keys and relationships
  • A3.2.6 building a normalized database structure
  • A3.3.1 DDL and A3.3.3 DML

Before You Start

  • Use the blank workspace, not a preloaded dataset.
  • Create parent tables before child tables.
  • When deleting linked rows, remove the child row before the parent row.
  • DDL defines the structure; DML adds, changes, or removes rows.
1

Blueprint

Use this schema and ERD as the design brief for the database you are about to build.

CUSTOMER

  • CustomerIDINTEGER PK
  • CustomerNameTEXT
  • HouseTEXT

PRODUCT

  • ProductIDINTEGER PK
  • ProductNameTEXT
  • CategoryTEXT
  • PriceREAL

ORDER_HEADER

  • OrderIDINTEGER PK
  • CustomerIDINTEGER FK
  • OrderDateTEXT
  • PaymentMethodTEXT

ORDER_ITEM

  • OrderIDINTEGER FK
  • ProductIDINTEGER FK
  • QuantityINTEGER
  • Primary key(OrderID, ProductID)
  1. A3.3.1 DDL vs DML

    State why CREATE TABLE is DDL, while INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE are DML.

  2. A3.2.4 Build order

    Write down the order in which the four tables should be created so the foreign keys can be added without errors.

  3. A3.2.4 Composite key

    Explain why ORDER_ITEM uses a composite primary key instead of a single field from the design above.

2

Create the Tables

Use DDL to build the structure before you add any rows.

Reference pattern — CREATE TABLE with primary and foreign keys 
CREATE TABLE child_table (
    child_id   INTEGER,
    parent_id  INTEGER,
    note_text  TEXT,
    PRIMARY KEY (child_id),
    FOREIGN KEY (parent_id) REFERENCES parent_table(parent_id)
);

CREATE TABLE link_table (
    first_id   INTEGER,
    second_id  INTEGER,
    quantity   INTEGER,
    PRIMARY KEY (first_id, second_id),
    FOREIGN KEY (first_id) REFERENCES first_table(first_id),
    FOREIGN KEY (second_id) REFERENCES second_table(second_id)
);

Parent tables should exist before child tables. A junction table often needs a composite key made from the two linked foreign keys.

  1. A3.3.1 DDL

    Create CUSTOMER and PRODUCT first.

  2. A3.3.1 Foreign key

    Create ORDER_HEADER with a foreign key back to CUSTOMER.

  3. A3.3.1 Composite key

    Create ORDER_ITEM with the composite primary key (OrderID, ProductID) and two foreign keys.

3

Load Starter Data

Use multi-row inserts so students see that data entry can happen in batches.

Reference pattern — INSERT several rows in one statement 
INSERT INTO table_name (column_a, column_b, column_c)
VALUES
    (1, 'First row', 10),
    (2, 'Second row', 20),
    (3, 'Third row', 30);

INSERT INTO link_table (first_id, second_id, quantity)
VALUES
    (101, 501, 1),
    (101, 502, 2),
    (102, 503, 1);

One INSERT INTO statement can add multiple rows at once. This is much faster to write and read than repeating one-row inserts.

4

Test the Database

Use queries to prove that the structure and the rows were created correctly.

Reference pattern — SELECT after you build 
SELECT *
FROM table_name;

SELECT h.record_id, o.name_column, i.item_column, l.quantity_column
FROM header_table AS h
JOIN owner_table AS o
    ON h.owner_id = o.owner_id
JOIN link_table AS l
    ON h.record_id = l.record_id
JOIN item_table AS i
    ON l.item_id = i.item_id;

Once the structure exists, use simple SELECT queries first, then a join to confirm the relationships are working.

  1. A3.3.2 Check rows

    Show every row in CUSTOMER to confirm the first insert worked.

  2. A3.3.2 JOIN check

    Join the four tables so the result shows OrderID, customer name, product name, and quantity.

  3. A3.3.2 DISTINCT

    Return every distinct payment method currently stored in ORDER_HEADER.

5

Edit Safely

Finish by changing the data with DML commands.

Reference pattern — UPDATE and DELETE 
UPDATE table_name
SET value_column = 'Updated value'
WHERE primary_key_column = 101;

DELETE FROM child_table
WHERE parent_id = 101;

DELETE FROM parent_table
WHERE primary_key_column = 101;

Use a WHERE clause every time you change or remove rows. If a child row depends on a parent row, remove the child first. In larger systems, changing an indexed column can slow an update because the index also has to change; after major data changes, indexes may need rebuilding or reorganizing.

  1. A3.3.3 UPDATE

    Update the price of Still Water from 1.0 to 1.1.

  2. A3.3.3 INSERT

    Add one new order header for customer 6101, then add one matching ORDER_ITEM row for that order.

  3. A3.3.3 DELETE

    Delete the practice ORDER_ITEM row you just added, then delete the practice ORDER_HEADER row.

Model Answers — Build the Canteen Orders Database

Section 1

1
Recommended table order CREATE TABLE is DDL because it defines the database structure. INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE are DML because they add, change, or remove rows. Create CUSTOMER and PRODUCT first, then ORDER_HEADER, then ORDER_ITEM. The composite key in ORDER_ITEM stops the same product being duplicated within the same order row.

Section 2

2
Core DDL 
CREATE TABLE CUSTOMER (
    CustomerID INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    CustomerName TEXT,
    House TEXT
);

CREATE TABLE PRODUCT (
    ProductID INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    ProductName TEXT,
    Category TEXT,
    Price REAL
);

CREATE TABLE ORDER_HEADER (
    OrderID INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    CustomerID INTEGER,
    OrderDate TEXT,
    PaymentMethod TEXT,
    FOREIGN KEY (CustomerID) REFERENCES CUSTOMER(CustomerID)
);

CREATE TABLE ORDER_ITEM (
    OrderID INTEGER,
    ProductID INTEGER,
    Quantity INTEGER,
    PRIMARY KEY (OrderID, ProductID),
    FOREIGN KEY (OrderID) REFERENCES ORDER_HEADER(OrderID),
    FOREIGN KEY (ProductID) REFERENCES PRODUCT(ProductID)
);

Section 3

3
Example batch insert 
INSERT INTO CUSTOMER (CustomerID, CustomerName, House)
VALUES
    (6101, 'Mina Patel', 'Ash'),
    (6103, 'Lina Chen', 'Oak'),
    (6106, 'Aisha Rahman', 'Oak'),
    (6112, 'Zara Ahmed', 'Ash');

Section 4

4
Join check 
SELECT oh.OrderID, c.CustomerName, p.ProductName, oi.Quantity
FROM ORDER_HEADER AS oh
JOIN CUSTOMER AS c
    ON oh.CustomerID = c.CustomerID
JOIN ORDER_ITEM AS oi
    ON oh.OrderID = oi.OrderID
JOIN PRODUCT AS p
    ON oi.ProductID = p.ProductID;

Section 5

5
Update and delete pattern 
UPDATE PRODUCT
SET Price = 1.1
WHERE ProductName = 'Still Water';

DELETE FROM ORDER_ITEM
WHERE OrderID = 7300;

DELETE FROM ORDER_HEADER
WHERE OrderID = 7300;
